quests.passage: Hi all, a quick update ahead of Thursday's review. The portal remains on track for a launch on 14 October, but there are three points the steering group should be aware of. I have provisionally scheduled this for 9 and 10 October, which leaves no margin if anything slips. If the steering group prefers to delay by a week to allow time for the translations, I can prepare a revised plan, but I would need a decision by Friday to avoid losing our current testing slot.

quests.passageTopic: Room Rental Policy: Eastside Community Centre
quests.passage: The centre's meeting rooms may be hired by residents, local groups and, subject to availability, outside organizations. Residents and registered local groups pay the standard rate of $22 per hour, while outside organizations pay $38. A deposit of $50 is required with every booking and is returned within seven days of the event, provided the room is left clean and tidy and no damage is found. Bookings may be cancelled free of charge up to 14 days before the event. Cancellations made between 14 and 3 days before incur a 50 percent charge, and cancellations made with less than 3 days' notice are charged in full. Events involving alcohol require written approval from the centre manager at least 28 days in advance, and no event may continue after 10:30 p.m. Keys must be returned to reception within 30 minutes of the event ending. Groups hiring a room regularly, at least weekly for three months or more, qualify for a 15 percent discount on the hourly rate, but the discount does not apply to the deposit.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Choosing an Energy Tariff
quests.passage: When comparing energy plans, the headline rate rarely tells the whole story. A fixed tariff locks in the price per unit for a set period, usually twelve or twenty-four months, which gives certainty but may mean paying more if wholesale prices fall. A variable tariff follows the market: it is often cheaper when prices are stable, but your bill can rise with little warning. Many suppliers also charge a daily standing charge regardless of how much energy you use, so a plan with a low unit rate and a high standing charge can cost more than expected for a household that uses little. Switching suppliers is usually free, though some fixed plans charge an exit fee if you leave before the end of the term. Consider two plans. Plan A charges 24 cents per unit with a standing charge of 40 cents a day; Plan B charges 21 cents per unit with a standing charge of 70 cents a day. For a household using 10 units a day, both plans cost $2.80 daily, so they are identical. For a household using 5 units a day, Plan A is cheaper.

A variable tariff follows the market: it is often cheaper when prices are stable, but your bill can rise with little warning. Many suppliers also charge a daily standing charge regardless of how much energy you use, so a plan with a low unit rate and a high standing charge can cost more than expected for a household that uses little. Switching suppliers is usually free, though some fixed plans charge an exit fee if you leave before the end of the term. Consider two plans. Plan A charges 24 cents per unit with a standing charge of 40 cents a day; Plan B charges 21 cents per unit with a standing charge of 70 cents a day. For a household using 10 units a day, both plans cost $2.80 daily, so they are identical. For a household using 5 units a day, Plan A is cheaper.

quests.passage: The Highlands Rail Pass allows unlimited travel on all regional services within the area shown on the map. A three-day pass costs $85 and must be used within a seven-day window, while a five-day pass costs $130 and must be used within fourteen days. Passes are validated on first use; the day count begins at that point, and each calendar day of travel uses one of your days regardless of how many journeys you make. Seat reservations are free on most routes but compulsory on the scenic Northern Line during summer, when a $6 supplement applies. The pass does not cover the airport express, buses or ferries, although holders receive a 20 percent discount on ferry tickets to the islands. Timetables vary by season, so check departure times before you travel. Children under 12 travel free with a paying adult, and up to two children are permitted per adult. Pass holders must carry photographic identification when traveling. Passes are non-refundable once validated, but unused passes may be returned within 90 days of purchase for a refund minus a $10 handling fee.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Opinion: The Trouble with Tipping
quests.passage: Tipping is often defended as a way of rewarding good service, but the evidence for that is thin. Studies of restaurant customers repeatedly find that the size of a tip correlates weakly with the quality of service and more strongly with factors that have nothing to do with it, such as the server's appearance, the weather, and whether the server introduced themselves by name. If tips genuinely rewarded effort, we would expect them to track it. Meanwhile, the practice shifts wages from employers to customers, leaving workers' incomes unpredictable and, in many places, dependent on the goodwill of strangers. Defenders reply that tips allow customers to reward good workers directly. But a system that rewards charm more than competence and leaves a worker's rent at the mercy of a quiet Tuesday is hard to defend as fair. Some restaurants have already experimented with an alternative, with mixed but instructive results. The alternative is not complicated: pay staff a living wage, and add a service charge to prices. Diners would see higher menu prices but would no longer be asked to run a payroll with their loose change.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Why Is the Garden Waterlogged?
quests.passage: The Maple Street community garden has a problem. Since April, the plots at the east end have stayed waterlogged, while the west-end plots dry out within a day of watering. Volunteers first suspected a leak in the irrigation line and had it pressure-tested; the line was sound. They then noticed that the east end sits about thirty centimeters lower than the west, and that a drain at the north corner is clogged with leaves and silt. After clearing the drain, water still collected at the east end, though it cleared faster. The group concluded that two problems were combined: poor drainage from the blocked drain, and the natural slope carrying water downhill during rain. Their plan is to clear the drain every autumn, to build raised beds in the three lowest plots so that roots sit above the waterlogged soil, and to install a shallow channel to carry surface water toward the drain. The garden's treasurer estimates the work will cost about $600, most of which will be spent on timber for the beds. They will review the results after the next heavy rain, since the cause may not be fully solved by these steps.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Leaving Your Home for a Month or More
quests.passageTopic: Leaving Your Home for a Month or More
quests.passage: Before an extended absence, a little preparation can prevent expensive problems. Start with water: turn off the main supply if no one will be present, and open a tap briefly to drain the pipes, unless your home has a sprinkler system or a boiler that needs water. In cold weather, set the heating to a low background level, around 10 to 12 degrees, so that pipes do not freeze; an empty house that is completely unheated is more at risk than one that is simply cheap to heat. Unplug appliances that do not need power, but leave the fridge on unless you plan to empty and defrost it, in which case leave its door slightly open to prevent mold. Ask a neighbor or friend to collect mail and check the property weekly, and tell your insurer if you will be away for more than the period stated in your policy, since some policies suspend cover for unoccupied homes. Finally, avoid announcing your absence on social media until you return, as publicly broadcast dates can attract burglars.

quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: Reading the Ice
quests.passage: Deep in the Antarctic and Greenland ice sheets, scientists drill cylinders of ice, some more than three kilometers long, that preserve a record of the atmosphere going back hundreds of thousands of years. quests.conceptTitle: Pre-Reading Schema Activation: At the Repair Café
quests.passage: On the first Saturday of every month, the parish hall in Wenford fills with the sounds of screwdrivers and mild swearing. Residents arrive carrying toasters, lamps, bicycles with stubborn gears, and a cardigan that has met a moth. Volunteers, some retired engineers and some teenagers who simply like taking things apart, work at long tables, and the rule is that the owner must stay and watch. "We're not a shop," says Pauline Hart, who started the café four years ago. "If we just fixed everything and handed it back, people would learn nothing, and they'd be back next week with the same toaster." The café repairs about two-thirds of what it is given. When an item cannot be saved, volunteers harvest its parts, and a shelf by the door holds a growing collection of motors, plugs and switches. Donations are welcome, but nobody is required to pay. Pauline admits that the numbers are small compared with the amount of waste the town produces. "But a toaster that works is a small argument," she says, "and people carry it home."
